695aed975242f618a4d2fa2f.statement: Design a writer class that holds an in-memory buffer of a fixed byte capacity in front of an output sink. write(data) appends the bytes in order; whenever the buffer becomes completely full it is immediately emptied into the sink, so a single long write can empty the buffer several times. flush() empties whatever is currently buffered, even if the buffer is not full. Because the real sink is not observable in a test, each method returns a new list of exactly the bytes passed to the sink during that call, or an empty list when nothing was passed. The class may also be given a sink object whose write(byte) method receives each byte as it is emptied.

requirements.text: The constructor takes a capacity of at least 1 and starts with an empty buffer.
write(data) appends bytes in their original order and empties the buffer into the sink every time it becomes exactly full, possibly more than once per call.
flush() empties all currently buffered bytes; with an empty buffer it hands nothing to the sink.
Every method returns a fresh list of the bytes handed to the sink during that call, in sink order; the constructor contributes null to a trace.
Bytes reach the sink in exactly the order they were written across all calls.
The input data lists are not modified.

constraints: capacity is between 1 and 10^4.
At most 10^4 method calls follow the constructor.
Each write carries 0 to 10^4 bytes, each in the range -128 to 127.
The total number of written bytes is at most 2*10^5.

approach.title: Fixed array buffer with a fill index, copying the largest fitting slice each step
approach.explanation: Keep a preallocated array of length capacity and an integer size that says how much of it is used. A write is processed in slices: take as many bytes as fit (the smaller of the free space and the remaining input), copy them in, advance, and if the buffer is now full, drain it to the sink and reset size to zero. Draining appends the buffered bytes to this call's output list (and, when a sink object was given, calls its write for each byte). flush drains only when size is positive. Each input byte is copied once into the buffer and once out, so a write costs time proportional to its length.
chooseWhen: Output is staged in fixed-size blocks and must be emitted as soon as a block fills.
You want memory bounded by the capacity regardless of how large a single write is.
You need the exact block boundaries, not just the final stream.
tradeoffs: Copying slices keeps the loop count per write at about len(data)/capacity + 1 instead of one iteration per byte.
A growable list that is cleared on drain is simpler but reallocates; the fixed array keeps memory at capacity.
Returning drained bytes as lists is a test model; a real implementation would hand whole blocks to the file instead of building output lists.
invariants: 0 <= size < capacity between calls: a full buffer never survives a call.
buffer[0:size] holds, in order, exactly the written bytes that have not yet reached the sink.
The concatenation of all returned lists followed by buffer[0:size] equals the concatenation of all written data.

stages.title: Implement write and flush over a fixed array
stages.question: How do you copy a write into the buffer without handling one byte per loop iteration and without exceeding capacity?
stages.explanation: Allocate buffer = [0]*capacity and size = 0. In write, loop while input remains: take = min(capacity - size, remaining), copy that slice into buffer[size:size+take], advance size and the input index, and drain if size == capacity. _drain appends buffer[0:size] to the call's output list, forwards each byte to an optional sink, and resets size. flush creates an output list and drains only when size > 0. The trace adapter builds one instance from the constructor row and records each method's result.
stages.rationale: Slice copies bound the iterations per write, and the shared drain helper keeps write and flush consistent.
instructions: Create the instance state: capacity, fixed buffer, size, optional sink.

hints: Compute take before copying so you never write past the end of the buffer.

approach.title: Post-order aggregation: a fully flagged subtree costs one operation
approach.explanation: Process directories bottom-up. For each directory compute three facts about its subtree: the minimum cost, how many files it contains, and whether all of them are flagged (clean). Start from the direct files (each flagged file costs 1 on its own; any unflagged file makes the subtree unclean), add the children's costs and file counts, and combine their clean flags. If the subtree has at least one file and is clean, one directory operation replaces everything, so the cost becomes 1. Otherwise a directory operation is forbidden and the cost is the sum. The root's cost is the answer. The traversal is done iteratively (an explicit stack produces a pre-order list that is processed in reverse) so depth 200 trees do not risk recursion limits.
chooseWhen: An operation applies to a whole subtree and is only allowed when every leaf below satisfies a condition.
Each subtree's best answer depends only on its children's answers.
Trees may be deep and you want to avoid recursion.
tradeoffs: Recursive post-order is shorter to write, but deep trees can hit recursion limits in Python.
Brute-force subset enumeration (the cohort's reference) is exact but exponential; the greedy subtree rule is linear.
Using node identity as a map key avoids mutating the input tree to store results.
invariants: When a directory is processed, all of its subdirectories have already been processed.
cost(dir) is the minimum number of allowed operations that encrypt exactly the flagged files in that subtree.
clean(dir) is true exactly when no unflagged file exists in the subtree.

approach.title: Tree DP over the inherited state
approach.explanation: What a node needs depends only on the state it inherits from the nearest operation above it: off (decrypted) or on (encrypted). Define cost(node, s) as the minimum operations inside the node's subtree given inherited state s. A file costs 0 if its flag equals s and 1 otherwise (one operation on the file fixes it). For a directory, either leave it alone, so children inherit s and the cost is the sum of children at s, or operate on it to switch to the other state, costing 1 plus the sum of children at not s. Operating to set the same state as inherited is never useful. The root inherits off, so the answer is cost(root, off). Computing both states bottom-up is linear.

Each subtree's best cost depends on a small piece of context passed from above.

tradeoffs: Enumerating none/encrypt/decrypt per node (the reference) is exact only for tiny trees.
Carrying two numbers per directory doubles the state but keeps one linear pass.
An iterative traversal avoids recursion depth issues at the cost of an explicit order list.
invariants: For each processed directory, keep_off and keep_on are the sums of children's costs when the inherited state is off or on.

approach.title: Digit-by-digit counting in base 4
approach.explanation: Fancy numbers with k base-4 digits correspond to k-bit binary masks, so fancy numbers below 4^k number 2^k (counting zero). Read n's base-4 digits from the most significant. At a position with r digits to its right: if n's digit is 0, a fancy number matching so far must also put 0 there; if it is 1, every fancy number that puts 0 there and anything in the lower r digits is smaller, adding 2^r, and we continue matching with 1; if it is 2 or 3, both 0 and 1 are allowed there with any lower digits, adding 2^(r+1), and no fancy number can match this digit, so we stop. The total counts fancy numbers in [0, n), including 0, so subtract 1.
chooseWhen: You count numbers below a bound whose digits come from a restricted set.
The bound is large but has few digits.
Each restricted digit set maps to a simple per-position count.
tradeoffs: Generating all fancy numbers below 4^15 and bisecting (the reference) is simple but uses about 2^16 values.
The digit scan uses O(log n) time and space but needs careful handling of the stop condition.
Counting zero and subtracting it at the end keeps the per-digit rule uniform.
invariants: Before processing a position, count equals the number of fancy values below n that differ from n at a higher position.
The prefix processed so far consists only of digits 0 and 1 while the scan continues.

approach.title: Trie of unsafe words, walked from every text position
approach.explanation: Insert every unsafe word into a trie and mark the nodes where words end. To test a text, start a walk at each position: follow the trie as long as the next character has a child, and report unsafe as soon as an end marker is reached. Because unsafe words are at most 20 characters long, each walk takes at most 20 steps, so a text of length L costs at most 20L steps regardless of how many unsafe words there are.

You want cost independent of the number of patterns.
Aho-Corasick would be overkill for the length bound.
tradeoffs: Running a substring search per word (the reference) costs about L times the number of words.
Aho-Corasick gives O(L) per text but is harder to implement correctly.
The trie uses memory proportional to the total length of the unsafe words.
invariants: During a walk from start, the current trie node spells text[start:i].
A message is marked unsafe only when the spelled prefix is a complete unsafe word.

approach.title: Pending buffer with a proper-prefix hold-back
approach.explanation: Keep a pending buffer consisting of the held-back suffix plus the new chunk. Precompute the set of proper prefixes of all stop words. After appending a chunk, find the hold position: the smallest start among the last (longest - 1) positions whose suffix is a proper prefix of some stop word. Search pending for the earliest complete stop word. If one starts at or before the hold position, it is certain: release text before it and stop. Otherwise release pending up to the hold position and keep the rest. At the end, flush what remains, cut at any stop word.

Holding back the smallest-start candidate suffix is conservative: it may delay text that turns out to be safe, but never releases unsafe text.
The prefix set uses memory proportional to the total stop-word length squared in the worst case (all proper prefixes).
